title: Train for Truth, Keep the Skills: Binary Retrieval-Augmented Reward Mitigates Hallucinations
claim: A binary retrieval-verified reward trains the policy to cut hallucination while preserving utility, beating other post-training baselines.
layout: 2 panels: left pipeline with worked example, right scatter plot with arrows
description: The left panel is a method diagram. A top row runs Training Data to a grey Policy node (π_θ) to a pink box defining the Binary Retrieval-augmented Reward, with r = 0 if contradiction and 1 otherwise. A feedback arrow loops from the reward back to the policy. Below it is a worked example. An instruction about Brent Crude Oil mean-reversion leads to (1) a response with code that uses the wrong ticker. (2) Retrieval then shows a document with the correct symbol BZ=F. (3) Verification gives a reason and Score: 0, with the errors in red. The right panel is a scatter plot of Utility (AlpacaEval) against Hallucination (Biography FactScore, inverted y-axis). Qwen3-8B is the base point. Colored dots for RL variants, DPO and SFT are connected to it by arrows. The red Binary RAR dot sits at the top, the best corner, and a faint 'Better' arrow marks the good direction.
caption: Overview of Binary Retrieval-Augmented Reward (Binary RAR). Left: Reinforcement learning with Binary RAR assigns a binary reward based on retrieval-verified factual correctness. Right: Binary RAR achieves the best hallucination–utility tradeoff among all post-training baselines.
abstract: Language models often generate factually incorrect information unsupported by their training data, a phenomenon known as extrinsic hallucination. Existing mitigation approaches often degrade performance on open-ended generation and downstream tasks, limiting their practical utility. We propose an online reinforcement learning method using a novel binary retrieval-augmented reward (RAR) to address this tradeoff. Unlike continuous reward schemes, our approach assigns a reward of one only when the model's output is entirely factually correct, and zero otherwise. We evaluate our method on Qwen3 reasoning models across diverse tasks. For open-ended generation, binary RAR achieves a 39.3% reduction in hallucination rates, substantially outperforming both supervised training and continuous-reward RL baselines. In short-form question answering, the model learns calibrated abstention, strategically outputting "I don't know" when faced with insufficient parametric knowledge. This yields 44.4% and 21.7% fewer incorrect answers on PopQA and GPQA, respectively. Crucially, these factuality gains come without performance degradation on instruction following, math, or code, whereas continuous-reward RL, despite improving factuality, induces quality regressions.
